questions.question: Which order matches the usual GitHub flow for a change?
options: Branch from `main` → commit → push the branch → open a pull request → review → merge → delete the branch
Commit on `main` → push → open a pull request → create a branch
Fork → commit on `main` → force-push → merge
Open a pull request → branch → commit → push → merge
questions.explanation: `main` always stays deployable, and every change goes through a short-lived branch and a reviewed pull request. Small, frequent pull requests are easier to review than large ones.

questions.question: Which Git command opens a pull request?
options: None: pull requests are a feature of hosting sites like GitHub and GitLab, not of Git itself
`git pull`
`git request-pull` creates the GitHub pull request
`git push --pr`
questions.explanation: You push a branch with Git, then open the pull request on the website, or with GitHub's own `gh pr create` command. Despite its name, `git pull` just fetches and merges. (`git request-pull` exists, but only prints a summary to e-mail.)

questions.question: A reviewer asks for changes on your open pull request. How do you update it?
options: Commit the changes on the same branch and push; the pull request updates automatically
Close the pull request and open a new one with the changes
Push the changes to `main`
Create a new branch for each round of review
questions.explanation: A pull request tracks a **branch**, not a fixed set of commits. Anything you push to it shows up in the pull request. If you rewrote the branch (rebase, amend), use `git push --force-with-lease`.

questions.question: While your pull request was open, `main` moved on and now there are conflicts. How do you bring your branch up to date locally?
options: `git fetch origin`, then `git rebase origin/main` (or `git merge origin/main`), fix conflicts and push
`git pull` while on your feature branch, without arguments
Merge the pull request anyway; GitHub fixes the conflicts
`git reset --hard origin/main`, then push
questions.explanation: Fetch first so `origin/main` is current. Rebasing gives a clean history but needs `--force-with-lease`; merging `main` in keeps history and needs a normal push. Ask your team which they prefer. `reset --hard` would throw away your work.

questions.question: What's the difference between forking and cloning?
options: A fork is your own copy of a repository **on GitHub**; a clone is a copy **on your computer**
They're the same; fork is GitHub's word for clone
A fork only copies the latest commit; a clone copies the history
A clone can be pushed to the original; a fork can't be pushed at all
questions.explanation: You fork when you can't push to the original project: you push to your fork and open a pull request from it. You then clone your fork to work on it locally, and add the original as the `upstream` remote.

questions.question: Your pull request was merged on GitHub with **Squash and merge**. Locally, `git branch -d feature` says the branch is not fully merged. Why?
options: Squashing created one new commit on `main`; your original commits are not in `main`'s history
GitHub hasn't finished merging yet
You need to run `git pull` on the feature branch first
Branches merged on GitHub can only be deleted on GitHub
questions.explanation: Git checks whether the branch's commits are reachable from `main`, and after a squash they aren't, even though the changes are. Once you've checked the pull request was merged, delete it with `git branch -D feature`.

questions.question: Your team uses Conventional Commits. Which message fits a bug fix?
options: `fix: round VAT to two decimals`
`feat: round VAT to two decimals`
`chore: fixed bug`
`bug(VAT) - fixed`
questions.explanation: The format is `type(optional scope): description`. Common types: `feat` (new feature), `fix` (bug fix), `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`. A `!` after the type, or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer, marks a breaking change. Tools can generate changelogs and version numbers from this.

questions.question: Why do experienced developers prefer small, focused commits?
options: They're easier to review, to revert on their own, and to pinpoint with `git bisect`
Git stores small commits more efficiently
Large commits are rejected by GitHub
Small commits don't need a message
questions.explanation: One logical change per commit means one commit to revert when something goes wrong, and a precise answer from `git bisect` and `git blame`. `git add -p` helps split mixed work into focused commits.

questions.question: How do you make GitHub close issue 42 automatically when your pull request is merged into the default branch?
options: Write `Fixes #42` (or `Closes #42`) in the pull request description
Name the branch `issue-42`
Add the label `42` to the pull request
Run `git close 42` before pushing
questions.explanation: GitHub recognises keywords such as `close`, `fix` and `resolve` (and their variants) followed by an issue reference, in the pull request description or in commit messages that land on the default branch.

questions.question: You paired with a colleague on a commit. How do you credit them so GitHub shows both of you as authors?
options: Add a trailer line `Co-authored-by: Name <email>` at the end of the commit message
Use `git commit --author` twice
Add their name to the branch name
Push the commit from both computers
questions.explanation: Trailers go after a blank line at the end of the message. The email must match one linked to their GitHub account. A commit can have only one author, so co-authorship is recorded this way.

questions.question: `git push` over HTTPS to GitHub asks for a password, and your account password is rejected. What should you use instead?
options: A personal access token, or switch the remote to SSH with an SSH key
Your password with `--force`
The email address instead of the username
`git config --global user.password`
questions.explanation: GitHub no longer accepts account passwords for Git operations. Use a personal access token as the password (a credential helper or the GitHub CLI can store it), or add an SSH key and use a `git@github.com:` URL. Git has no `user.password` setting.

questions.question: You want to run pull request 57 locally, but it comes from someone else's fork. Which command fetches it into a local branch `pr-57`?
options: `git fetch origin pull/57/head:pr-57`
`git pull origin 57`
`git switch pr/57`
`git clone --pr 57`
questions.explanation: GitHub exposes every pull request on the base repository as the ref `refs/pull/<n>/head`, even when it comes from a fork. The refspec `pull/57/head:pr-57` fetches it into a new local branch. With the GitHub CLI: `gh pr checkout 57`.

questions.question: Your team wants to make sure nobody pushes directly to `main` and every change is reviewed and passes CI. Where is this enforced?
options: On the hosting side, with branch protection rules (or rulesets) for `main`
In each developer's `.gitconfig`
In the `.gitignore` file
With a `pre-commit` hook in `.git/hooks`
questions.explanation: Branch protection on GitHub can require pull requests, approvals, passing status checks and linear history, and block force-pushes. Local hooks and settings can be skipped or are never shared, so they can't enforce a team rule.
